toc.title: Polyvagal Theory is not a prescription

sections.title: Build the strength of your safety state

blocks.p: A listener replied to one of my emails, where I'd asked what people want to know about. Here's what she wrote:

q: A topic I really think would be of interest to me, if you haven't already covered it, is performance anxiety. For example, the other day I played a piano jazz piece on Zoom before 40 other students, including our jazz piano teacher. My hands shook so much from stage fright that it made it quite difficult to play. What's a good approach to use polyvagal theory for this?

blocks.h: Polyvagal Theory is not a prescription

blocks.p: First, the question: what's a good approach to use Polyvagal Theory for this? I don't know if she meant it this way, but Polyvagal Theory is not a modality. It's not a prescription. It doesn't exactly say what you should do, how you should handle things, or what your behaviors should be. I think it helps us understand how to optimize ourselves on a biological level, a nervous system level. It can help us feel more safety and more connection. There are principles we can pull from it, but in no way is it telling us how to behave.

People like me take our understanding of the science of the Polyvagal Theory and pull from it. I applied it to my own understanding of mental health and trauma recovery as a therapist, and created my system. But the Polyvagal Theory itself is just science. It explains what's happening within us on a biological level when we do things like hug each other, and also when we do things like have stage fright while playing piano on a Zoom call. It doesn't say what to do. It says: here's what's happening, and I can explain this.
I can't speak for this listener. I don't know what's happening within her. But I can speak on a more general level.

This actually happened to my daughter. She plays piano, and at her last recital, in front of 50 people or so, the same thing happened. I was close by, filming, and you could see her tense up, and her hands started shaking. She got through it, but you could tell she was really struggling.

What's likely happening on a nervous system level is that the person is losing access to their safety state. When we lose access to the safety state, our defensive states become dominant. We become dysregulated. Without the safety state active, flight, fight, shutdown, and freeze start to flavor the system. They flavor our thoughts and our behaviors, or at least the range of what's possible: our thoughts, behaviors, and emotions, our ability to connect with others, our ability to perform piano in front of others. It all gets restricted. In flight or fight, we want to run away or be aggressive. In shutdown, we collapse and have a pull toward immobility, isolation, and lower stimulation. In freeze, we freeze. We tense up.

I can relate to this on a pretty big level. I don't like heights very much, especially when I'm in my car. Bridges where I can't see the ground, just blue sky on a steep bridge, or the drop-off when I'm driving on a cliff: that puts me into a little freeze. Cars and heights are not a good combination for me.

So what I saw in my daughter, and what I think is likely happening in general, is that the person loses access to their safety state and enters a freeze. The hand shaking is potentially the freeze itself, or the body's attempt to come out of freeze and shake it off. I'm not sure which it is for any one person. It could be either. But that muscle tension and shaking is likely a freeze state.

Shutdown, at the extreme, would be passing out, or dissociation. And part of freeze is shutdown. Freeze is a mixed state: a combination of flight or fight plus shutdown. The body is mobilized to run away or fight, but also immobilizing in shutdown. So freeze is immobile, but with flight and fight in the system, it's like hitting the accelerator and the brake at the same time in your car. The engine's revving, but it's not going anywhere. The wheels are just spinning. The hand shaking, the tension, not being able to focus, possibly a little or a lot of dissociation: that's likely a freeze reaction.
It could be a number of things, and maybe not one of them alone would trigger the freeze, but all of them combined could.

The moment itself. You're performing in front of a bunch of people. You might have a lot of pressure on you. You might have family expectations or cultural expectations. You might have a teacher who has been driving you up until this moment, and now it's all on you. Maybe the moment is just too big.

The cues from the audience. If you're playing in front of people who are staring blankly or have lost interest, chatting in the crowd, not looking at you, not smiling, those cues send danger cues to the person up there, who is probably already tense and feeling pressured. The faces in the crowd are strangers, and they're not friendly, warm, or inviting. Maybe they're flat out disinterested, chit-chatting with their own kids, wanting to leave. They're probably not angry or aggressive. It's not really danger, but our body detects it as dangerous through something called neuroception.

Being alone with a screen. If you're performing or presenting through Zoom, you're alone. You're talking to a screen. There are faces there, and that helps as long as they're engaged, but a lot of them might just be black screens with a name on them. You're talking into the void, kind of like I'm doing right now as I record this. Even though there are live people watching, they're not there with you. You can't hear their voices giving you encouragement. You can't reach out and hug someone who might otherwise comfort you.

The environment around you. If you're on a Zoom call, are you in a space where you actually feel some safety, connection, and groundedness? Or are you performing in a church or a community center where it's not your space? You don't feel comfortable there. You don't set the lighting or the temperature. You don't have control over the space, and that in itself can be dysregulating. Maybe there's something there you didn't plan on, and it causes some anxiety that contributes to the freeze.

For my daughter, the first time she performed, they gave her a keyboard and piano hybrid instead of the piano she practices on, and it threw her off. She got through it. The second time, she knew it was going to happen, and she had practiced on a keyboard, and that might have added to the pressure. Not having control over the environment, the instrument, all the pieces of it, might not be enough to tip you into dysregulation on its own, but it might contribute.

blocks.h3: Build the strength of your safety state

blocks.p: In general, to address freeze, or any defensive state, flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, it helps to develop the strength of your safety state. That means you prioritize feelings of connection: being grounded in the present moment, the experience of mindfulness, connection with other people, with yourself, and with your environment.

That doesn't mean everybody does what you want. It means you look inward and notice: what do I feel a pull toward? What brings feelings of positivity? What feels like connection, or freedom, or being grounded in the present moment? That's what we're aiming for.

Feeling connected to your pet is a lot different from feeling protected by hiding in your room in the dark by yourself. That's not safety. Connection with your pet, connection with yourself through your senses, connection with a loved one if you have one, connection with a professional like a therapist: those are the safety experiences we want to identify, practice, and mindfully experience, to build the strength of your safety state.

Then, as you do that, allow some defensive activation. If you know you're stuck in flight or fight, or in freeze or shutdown, anchor in safety, and then allow yourself to feel a tolerable amount of that defensive state. Doing that strengthens your safety state and softens the intensity of the defensive state. Over time it can reduce significantly, to the point where it's not debilitating, and you may just flat out recover from it.

More specifically for something like this: know what the environment is going to be like and what tools you'll have. What kind of keyboard or piano is it? How many seats are there? What's the lighting like? Who's going to be there? How many people will have their cameras on or off, and can you ask them to turn them on? When I give my trauma presentations over Zoom, I prefer to see people's faces, so I ask people to leave their cameras on.

If it's a Zoom performance, can you set up your own environment with cues of safety? As I record this, I'm mostly surrounded by things that bring me calm and cues of safety and connection: Lego, 49ers stuff, Polyvagal Theory books. Stuff I like. The light back here is soft and warm, and I like that kind of lighting. There's a mess you can't see, which I don't like, but in general it helps me feel good.
What can you control? What can you change? And if you can't, can you introduce your system to it ahead of time, so it's not a surprise when you get there?

There might also be some top-down things you can do. If you know you're going to go into freeze, tell yourself ahead of time: "I'm safe. I've rehearsed this. I can do this. I'm competent. People are here because they're excited about my talent, or my knowledge, or my speaking ability."

I don't like prescribed breathing too much, but when it comes to freeze, a slow exhale seems to help. When my therapy clients get into that tense, anxious flight or fight, or even freeze energy, I'll ask them, "Hey, can you breathe?" That prompts them, and they'll say, "Oh, yeah." They look inward and take that breath in and out. I think a bigger breath helps, especially if you exhale a little more slowly on the way out. That helps activate the safety state.

Have the thing down as much as you possibly can. When I first started doing my trauma and Polyvagal Theory presentations, I rehearsed them a number of times to make sure they fit in the time window, with breaks, and breaks in my speaking for Q&A. Rehearse the heck out of it. With sports or piano especially, muscle memory can go a long way.
If you combine that with the other things here, I'd say the potential for going into a dysregulated freeze state is probably lower overall.

But I don't know you, so ultimately you'll have to figure it out for yourself. What helps you feel safe? What helps you feel more grounded? What helps you feel more confident? These are just my ideas.
